doc.title: Alan Raph interviewed by Monk Rowe, Danbury, Connecticut, November 20, 2001

title: Professional jockeying, personalities and being easy to work with
summary: Raph says jockeying for position is universal and that contractors hire people they like. He praises Milt Hinton, Joe Wilder and Clark Terry as great musicians and nice people.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: It’s curious, I was talking to my daughter this weekend, she had done an area all-state type thing and was complaining about certain people who were sitting next to her because she was first chair, and there was some sniping.

She is a French hornist. And there was some, you know, what did you get on your NYSSMA, that kind of thing. And I said, “You know, that kind of thing probably goes all the way up to the top.” And am I right in that?
In what way? I’m not sure I follow.
I’m just wondering if in the classical world, or even in the jazz world, is there a certain amount of professional jealousy or kind of jockeying for position.

Yeah. But that’s in life. In life there is jockeying for position. Everything you do there is jockeying for position. The corporate, down to freelance, down to whatever you get into, there is always this. And unfortunately people come into New York or come into the business with the idea that their instrument and their ability and their talent is going to carry them and that should make them a star. And they get very, very perturbed when they find out that the business suddenly looms its ugly face and they have to cope with the business. They have to cope with, as they say on your report card in public schools, working and playing well with others. You know, they have to cope with this. And a lot of them are really, and this is jazz and symphonic and whatever, commercial musicians, a © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

lot of them are really not aware of being a person as well as being a musician. And those that learn do better than those that don’t learn. Many people come into town with a — we’ll call it an attitude. And they go out of town with the same attitude. But they go out of town.
Yeah. So a contractor, if he’s looking at his list of people to call, he will also be considering their personalities.

Oh, you better believe it. Absolutely. You can get, given the bass trombone, you can get five guys to play the bass trombone part. And two of them will argue with you. So they’re not going to get called. The third guy might not show up on time. So he’s not going to get called. Leaving two. And out of the two, well so-and-so is a nicer guy than so-and-so. You know? All playing being equal. All five of them can play the same let’s say. But you’re going to go with somebody that just kind of rubs you the right way. Absolutely.
I guess Milt Hinton was the classic example of—

Milt was absolutely wonderful. There’s nobody that doesn’t love Milt Hinton. Just like Joe Wilder. There’s nobody that doesn’t love Joe. There are certain people that are around here that are just absolutely brilliant musicians and the nicest people in the world.
Right. They make you feel good to be with them.
Oh Milt was a sweetheart. Clark Terry is another. There are so many.
